title: Decision Quality Index
tagline: 18 questions. 5 minutes. A precise read on how you actually make decisions — and where your thinking breaks down under pressure.
instructions: Answer based on how you actually decide — not how you wish you did.

_distinctness.consensus-seeker: Avoids being wrong by avoiding deciding.
_distinctness.loudest-voice: Defers to whoever speaks first or hardest.
_distinctness.calibrated-decider: Matches speed and rigor to the stakes; no trap dominant.

dimensions.label: Speed
dimensions.description: How quickly you move from new information to a decision.

scoreBands.narrative: You're losing decisions to delay. The cost of not deciding isn't on the books, but it's real.
Speed varies by topic and mood. Predictability is low.
Speed is matched to stakes. Reversible calls happen fast; high-impact ones get rigor.

dimensions.label: Information
dimensions.description: How well you incorporate evidence into the decision.

scoreBands.narrative: You're flying on gut. Sometimes right, but not for the reasons you think.
You gather data when it's easy and skip it when it's not. The hardest decisions get the least information.
You go after the data you need and stop gathering when more wouldn't change the call.

dimensions.label: Calibration
dimensions.description: How well your confidence in a decision matches your actual track record on calls of that type.

scoreBands.narrative: Your confidence outruns your accuracy. You don't know what you don't know — and your team can't tell you.
You're calibrated on familiar calls; overconfident on edge ones. The cost shows up on the unusual decisions.
You can tell the difference between 'I know this' and 'I'm pattern-matching from limited data.' Rare and valuable.

dimensions.label: Review
dimensions.description: How often and how honestly you revisit decisions after the outcome is known.

scoreBands.narrative: You're not learning from your decisions. Same mistakes will keep showing up.
You review the big ones, sometimes. The small-but-frequent decisions go unexamined.
You separate outcome from process. You can ask 'did I decide well even though the outcome was bad' (or vice versa).

archetypes.name: The Gut-Caller
archetypes.summary: You decide fast. You trust your read. You've been right enough times that you've stopped checking. The risk is that your gut is calibrated to the patterns you've seen — and the next high-stakes call may sit outside that pattern.
archetypes.blindSpot: Your accuracy is in the rooms you've been in. Unfamiliar rooms are where gut-callers go wrong.
nextMoves: Before your next high-stakes decision, write down two pieces of data that would change your answer. Go find them.
Build a 'when I'd want a second opinion' filter and use it for decisions outside your usual pattern.
Run a post-mortem on your three worst decisions of the past 12 months. What did your gut miss?

archetypes.name: The Over-Analyst
archetypes.summary: You make better decisions than most — when you finish them. The problem is the windows you've missed waiting for more data. Quality is real. So is the cost of not deciding.
archetypes.blindSpot: Inaction is a decision. You're making it without acknowledging the trade.
nextMoves: Set a hard deadline on your next decision in progress. Pick the date now.
For each pending decision, ask: what would more data actually change? If 'nothing,' decide today.
Track the cost of your last three delays in dollars, opportunity, or morale.

archetypes.name: The Consensus-Seeker
archetypes.summary: You bring people in. You hear them out. You also let the meeting end without a decision because no one was clearly aligned. The team starts to read you as someone who won't commit — which costs you more than being wrong would.
archetypes.blindSpot: Consensus is rarer than you think; alignment is what most groups can actually offer. They're not the same thing.
nextMoves: Distinguish consensus from alignment in your next decision meeting. Tell the room which one you need.
Pick one stalled decision. Make it this week, even if not everyone is fully on board.
Practice saying 'I've heard you. I'm deciding X. Here's why.'

archetypes.name: The Deferrer
archetypes.summary: Your decisions track whoever speaks first, longest, or most forcefully in the room. You'd say you weigh inputs — but the timing and intensity of those inputs is doing more work than the substance.
archetypes.blindSpot: Confidence is not evidence. The most confident person in the room is often the least calibrated.
nextMoves: For your next call, write your answer down before the discussion. Compare after.
Solicit the quietest person's view first in your next decision meeting.
Identify one decision in the past month where you went with the loudest voice. Audit the outcome.

archetypes.name: The Calibrator
archetypes.summary: You're matching speed to stakes. You gather the data you need and stop. You can name when you're guessing. This is the rarest archetype — and the easiest to slip out of when the pressure rises.
archetypes.blindSpot: Your calibration is hard-won. It's also easy to lose. The pressure that erodes it is usually invisible until it's too late.
nextMoves: Once a quarter, hand-pick five decisions and audit your reasoning quality vs. outcome. Watch for drift.
Identify the type of decision you're least calibrated on. Spend the next 90 days improving there.
Mentor someone less calibrated. Teaching it is how you protect it.

questions.text: I match decision speed to the stakes — small reversible decisions move fast.
I have decisions that have been sitting open for weeks longer than they should.
When a window is closing, I can name the cost of waiting in concrete terms.
I make most decisions in the last 24 hours before they're due, regardless of how long I've had to think about them.
For an important decision, I can name the two or three pieces of information that would most change my answer.
I tend to make calls based on what's familiar rather than what's relevant.
I actively seek out the perspective most likely to disagree with mine.
When data is hard to gather, I usually decide without it.
I can tell the difference between 'I know this' and 'I'm pattern-matching from limited data.'
I'm typically more confident in my decisions than the outcomes warrant.
I can name a recent decision where I was wrong — and what I missed.
When someone challenges my reasoning, my first instinct is to defend.
I revisit my big decisions a few months later to see how they played out.
If a decision had a bad outcome, I assume the decision was bad — without checking the process.
I keep track of decisions I was confident about that turned out wrong.
I rarely talk about my decision-making process with anyone — I just make the calls.
When you made your last hard call, the dominant input was:

options.label: My read of the situation — I knew what to do.
The data — I waited until the numbers were clear.
The conversation — I needed everyone aligned.
The strongest argument in the room.

questions.text: Looking back at a recent decision you got wrong, the most accurate diagnosis is:

options.label: I trusted my gut on something outside my pattern.
I waited too long for more information.
I let the group dynamic decide for me.
I went along with whoever was most insistent.

totalBands.label: Decision drag
totalBands.narrative: Decision quality is costing you. Pick the lowest-scoring dimension below — that's the leverage point. Pair the score with your archetype to see the specific trap.

totalBands.label: Mixed signal
totalBands.narrative: You're solid on some dimensions and exposed on others. Your archetype tells you which trap is most likely to surface under pressure.

totalBands.label: Calibrated
totalBands.narrative: You're decision-healthy across the board. The work now is protecting it. Calibration erodes under pressure — and the pressure rarely warns you it's eroding.
